result:
**Short answer:** yes, this is standard, and your description is fair provided the cycle is coherently oriented and you note that the bound girth ≤ P needs a step inside an orbit (or a cycle among orbits).

## (1) Closest standard statements

- **Symbolic dynamics (confident).** Solutions on a coherently oriented k-cycle are the closed walks of length k in the digraph of A, so their number is tr(A^k). This is the count of period-k points of the vertex shift (Lind & Marcus, *An Introduction to Symbolic Dynamics and Coding*, §2.2). "Locks" is exactly tr(A^k) = |W|: only the fixed points coming from the diagonal.
- **Graph homomorphisms (confident).** Solutions are homomorphisms from the directed cycle C_k to the reflexive digraph (W, A); a homomorphism from C_k exists exactly where there is a closed walk of length k (Hell & Nešetřil, *Graphs and Homomorphisms*). Your statement is "every homomorphism from C_k is constant iff k < directed girth of A minus the diagonal".
- **The limiting case (confident).** Infinite girth means A minus the diagonal is acyclic, i.e. the transitive closure of A is a partial order. Then every cycle locks; this is just antisymmetry (x_0 ≤ x_1 ≤ … ≤ x_0 forces equality). Your result is the finite-girth version of that.
- **CSP consistency (confident).** Composition along a path is Montanari's path-consistency calculus (1974), and tree-structured instances are decided by arc consistency (Freuder 1982). With A reflexive every instance is arc consistent, so arc consistency never sees the lock. It is a treewidth-2 fact, seen by path consistency.
- **Feder–Vardi (confident on the idea).** The universal cover of the cycle is the two-way infinite path, and tree duality only sees the cover. This is the precise sense of "forced on cycles but on no path".
- **Reflexive digraph homotopy (fairly confident).** Larose & Tardif, "A discrete homotopy theory for binary reflexive structures" (Adv. Math., c. 2004), is the nearest setting where non-constant cycles in reflexive structures are studied. I do not know a named theorem there that is literally yours.
- **Voltage graphs (confident on the framework, with a caveat).** When the shift acts freely on W, A is the derived graph of the quotient W/shift with voltages in Z_P (Gross & Tucker, *Topological Graph Theory*). A closed walk in the quotient lifts to a closed walk iff its net voltage is 0. Orbits of smaller minimal period break freeness, so there the net voltage must vanish modulo the orbit size instead.
- **Clock models.** "Winding number mod P" is the same net-voltage condition, but I am unsure of a specific citable statement.

I believe the statement itself is folklore rather than a named theorem.

## (2) Is the description fair? Subtleties

- **Orientation of the cycle matters.** The claim holds only for a coherently oriented cycle. If the cycle has at least one forward and one backward constraint, it never locks once A has any non-diagonal pair (u, v): put u on one arc between the two reversed constraints and v on the other.
- **Symmetric pairs kill it.** If (u, v) and (v, u) are both in A, the girth is 2 and nothing locks beyond k = 1. The phenomenon needs an antisymmetric A.
- **The bound girth ≤ P assumes a non-diagonal step inside one orbit.** If all non-diagonal steps go between different orbits and the quotient on orbits is acyclic, the girth is infinite. If the quotient has a cycle of length m with net shift d, you get girth ≤ m·P/gcd(d, P), not P.
- **Pendant copies are harmless, but only because A is reflexive.** Any partial assignment on a subtree extends by copying values, so the pair at distance d on a tree ranges over exactly A^d. Without the diagonal, pendants would prune values with no in- or out-neighbour.
- **"Tie" should mean equality.** On a path A itself is still forced at d = 1; what is never forced is equality (unless A is the diagonal).
- **Above the girth the cycle still constrains.** For k ≥ girth, (x_0, x_j) ranges over A^j ∩ (A^(k−j))^(−1), which can be strictly smaller than A^j. So the cycle forces more than any path at every length; only the full tie stops at the girth.
- **Padding.** "Locks iff k < girth" uses the diagonal to pad a shortest cycle with loops up to any k ≥ girth. Without reflexivity the answer would depend on which lengths of closed walk occur, not just the shortest.
